claims.claim: Dal Bó & Fréchette (AER 2011) find that in the infinitely repeated PD, cooperation can prevail, but only under conditions stricter than 'cooperation is a subgame-perfect equilibrium', and stricter even than a risk-dominance condition.
claims.quote: We show that cooperation may prevail in infinitely repeated games, but the conditions under which this occurs are more stringent than the subgame perfect conditions usually considered or even a condition based on risk dominance.
claims.source_title: Dal Bó & Fréchette, The Evolution of Cooperation in Infinitely Repeated Games: Experimental Evidence, AER 101(1):411-29
claims.notes: Quote is the AER abstract, fetched raw from aeaweb.org. Published February 2011, DOI 10.1257/aer.101.1.411.

claims.claim: Design of Dal Bó & Fréchette 2011: continuation probability δ ∈ {1/2, 3/4}, cooperation payoff R ∈ {32, 40, 48}. Each subject played between 23 and 77 repeated games. Grim risk-dominates AD in only 3 of the 6 cells (δ=1/2 & R=48; δ=3/4 & R=40; δ=3/4 & R=48). Cooperation is an SPE in every cell except δ=1/2 & R=32.
claims.quote: each subject participated in between 23 and 77 infinitely repeated games
claims.source_title: Dal Bó & Fréchette, working paper version (April 2007), Brown Econ WP 2007-7
claims.notes: Taken from the 2007 working paper (Table 3 and text), not the final AER text. The δ=0 one-shot control treatments are omitted here. Footnote 5 of the WP has an apparent typo ('R=23'). Check against the AER version before citing exact cells.

claims.claim: In Dal Bó & Fréchette 2011, first-round cooperation in the risk-dominant treatments rose from 46.5% in early repeated games to 70.6% after 110 interactions. When cooperation was not an equilibrium, first-round cooperation fell from 29% (games starting in the first 10 interactions) to 5.5%.
claims.quote: While in the first rounds of the early repeated games in the risk-dominant treatments cooperation was 46.5%, in later repeated games (after 110 interactions) it reached 70.6%
claims.source_title: Dal Bó & Fréchette 2007 WP (later AER 2011)
claims.notes: WP numbers; the published version may differ slightly. Strategy fits in the same WP: in late games, AD explains 90% of observations under δ=1/2,R=32 and Grim explains 93% under δ=3/4,R=48.

claims.claim: The Dal Bó & Fréchette JEL survey (2018) is a meta-analysis of experiments on the infinitely repeated PD. Being supportable in equilibrium does not mean most subjects cooperate. High cooperation appears only when cooperation is 'very robust to strategic uncertainty'.
claims.quote: However, the fact that cooperation can be supported in equilibrium does not imply that most subjects will cooperate. High cooperation rates will emerge only when the parameters of the repeated game are such that cooperation is very robust to strategic uncertainty.
claims.source_title: Dal Bó & Fréchette, On the Determinants of Cooperation in Infinitely Repeated Games: A Survey, JEL 56(1):60-114
claims.notes: Abstract fetched raw from aeaweb.org.

claims.claim: Size of the survey's meta-dataset: 15 papers, 32 treatments (δ, g, ℓ combinations), 2,415 subjects, 157,170 choices. Half the treatments, 73% of subjects and 67% of choices come from papers co-authored by the survey authors, who report robustness checks for this.
claims.quote: We have data from 15 papers, involving 32 different treatments (combinations of δ, g and ℓ), with 2415 subjects and a total of 157,170 choices.
claims.source_title: Dal Bó & Fréchette survey, working draft dated March 3, 2016 (Wayback copy)
claims.notes: From the 2016 draft. The published JEL 2018 version may have updated counts. The original Brown URL now 404s.

claims.claim: SizeBAD is the size of the basin of attraction of AD against Grim: the minimum belief that the other player is playing Grim needed for cooperation to be optimal. It equals 1 when cooperation is not an SPE, equals 1/2 when δ = δ_RD, and falls as δ rises. The survey adopts it as the main predictor of cooperation.
claims.quote: if SizeBAD = 0.8, a player needs to believe that the other player will cooperate with probability 0.8 or higher for him or her to want to also cooperate. If cooperation cannot be supported in equilibrium, then SizeBAD = 1
claims.source_title: Dal Bó & Fréchette survey (2016 draft)
claims.notes: Formula: SizeBAD = (1-δ)ℓ / (1-(1-δ)(1+g-ℓ)) if δ ≥ g/(1+g), else 1. The survey says it focuses on SizeBAD over δ-δ_RD 'due to its better' performance, but admits the data cannot clearly separate the two.

claims.claim: Strategies under perfect monitoring: AD, Grim and TFT account for most behaviour. Together they are the majority in 15 of 17 treatments and at least 70% in 11 of them. WSLS (Pavlov) is 'never a sizeable fraction'. AC is rare.
claims.quote: WSLS (not listed in this table), also known as Perfect TFT ... However, it is never a sizeable fraction of the strategies used.
claims.source_title: Dal Bó & Fréchette survey (2016 draft), Table 10 and Result 6
claims.notes: The quote is abridged with '...'. Also: 'Given the work of Axelrod, one could have expected subjects to use TFT. On the other hand, TFT is not subgame perfect, and, thus, Grim may be more likely. In fact, both Grim and TFT are present in the data.' This is useful nuance: humans use TFT, but not exclusively, and Grim is just as common.

claims.claim: The survey notes that across its 32 treatments, five pure strategies (AD, AC, Grim, TFT, STFT) always account for the majority of play. In supergames after the fourth, they cover 84% of play in supergames longer than one round. This counters Breitmoser's (2015) mixed-strategy reading.
claims.quote: for supergames greater than four, those five strategies account for 84 percent of play in supergames lasting more than one round and 79 percent of play in supergames lasting more than two rounds.
claims.source_title: Dal Bó & Fréchette survey (2016 draft), footnote 38
claims.notes: This finding is contested: Breitmoser 2015 AER 'Cooperation, but no reciprocity' argues for semi-grim / mixed behaviour. Worth a counter-check.

claims.claim: Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber (AER 2012): when intended actions are implemented with noise, subjects cooperate far more in treatments where cooperation is an equilibrium. Successful strategies are 'lenient' (do not retaliate for the first defection), and many are 'forgiving' (return to cooperation after punishing).
claims.quote: In these treatments successful strategies were "lenient" in not retaliating for the first defection, and many were "forgiving" in trying to return to cooperation after inflicting a punishment.
claims.source_title: Fudenberg, Rand & Dreber, Slow to Anger and Fast to Forgive: Cooperation in an Uncertain World, AER 102(2):720-49
claims.notes: Abstract fetched raw. The abstract also says 'considerable strategic diversity, indicating that subjects had not fully learned the distribution of play.'

claims.claim: FRD 2012 parameters: δ = 7/8 and noise probability 1/8 (an intended move is flipped to the other action). The survey's table lists FRD 2012 as δ=0.875, g=ℓ=0.33 (i.e. b/c=4) with 48 subjects in that cell. SFEM estimates for that cell: AC 24%, AD 6%, Grim 12%, TFT 15%, totalling only 57%. The rest are lenient or forgiving variants such as TF2T.
claims.source_title: Dal Bó & Fréchette survey (2016 draft), Tables 3 & 10, citing FRD 2012
claims.notes: Could NOT reach the FRD full text (Harvard DASH returned 429). δ=7/8 and the table numbers come from the survey. 'Noise = 1/8' and the full list of b/c values (believed to be 1.5/2/2.5/4) are from memory and need checking against the AER paper. One search snippet garbled the noise levels as '1/16 and 1/18', which is unreliable.

claims.claim: Wilkinson (Nature 1984), wild vampire bats (Desmodus rotundus): food sharing by blood regurgitation depends 'equally and independently' on relatedness and on an index of opportunity for reciprocation. Captive experiments showed that unrelated bats reciprocally exchange blood.
claims.quote: food sharing by regurgitation of blood among wild vampire bats (Desmodus rotundus) depends equally and independently on degree of relatedness and an index of opportunity for reciprocation.
claims.source_title: Wilkinson, Reciprocal food sharing in the vampire bat, Nature 308:181-184
claims.notes: Published March 1984. The abstract does not say 'tit-for-tat'. Whether the bat case is TFT is a later gloss (Axelrod and others).

claims.claim: Carter & Wilkinson (Proc B 2013): 20 captive vampire bats were fasted individually, inducing food sharing on 48 days over 2 years. Food received was the best predictor of food given, 8.5 times more important than relatedness. 64% of sharing dyads were unrelated (67% expected without nepotism). Donors initiated sharing more often than recipients, which argues against harassment.
claims.quote: Food received was the best predictor of food given across dyads, and 8.5 times more important than relatedness. Sixty-four per cent of sharing dyads were unrelated, approaching the 67 per cent expected if nepotism was absent.
claims.source_title: Carter & Wilkinson, Food sharing in vampire bats: reciprocal help predicts donations more than relatedness or harassment, Proc R Soc B
claims.notes: Abstract via Europe PMC. Framed as 'mutual direct fitness benefits' and social bonding, not as strict TFT.

claims.claim: Carter et al. (Current Biology 2020): previously unfamiliar captive vampire bats were tracked for 15 months. They selectively escalated low-cost grooming before forming higher-cost food-sharing relationships, which supports a 'raising-the-stakes' model. This is a relationship and bonding model, not round-by-round TFT.
claims.quote: We found compelling evidence that vampire bats selectively escalate low-cost grooming before developing higher-cost food-sharing relationships.
claims.source_title: Carter, Farine, Crisp, Vrtilek, Ripperger & Page, Development of New Food-Sharing Relationships in Vampire Bats, Curr Biol
claims.notes: Abstract via Europe PMC.

claims.claim: Milinski (Nature 1987): using mirrors, a single three-spined stickleback inspecting a live predator was given either a simulated cooperating companion (parallel mirror) or a simulated defecting one (angled mirror). In both cases the test fish behaved according to TIT FOR TAT.
claims.quote: In both cases the test fish behaved according to TIT FOR TAT supporting the hypothesis that cooperation can evolve among egoists.
claims.source_title: Milinski, TIT FOR TAT in sticklebacks and the evolution of cooperation, Nature 325:433-435
claims.notes: Published January 1987. The 'parallel vs angled mirror' detail is from my memory of the paper. The abstract says only 'a system of mirrors'.

claims.claim: Milinski's TFT interpretation was challenged right away. Lazarus & Metcalfe (Animal Behaviour 1990) published 'Tit-for-tat cooperation in sticklebacks: a critique of Milinski', and Milinski replied 'No alternative to TIT FOR TAT in sticklebacks' (Anim Behav 39:989-991). Masters & Waite (1990) also disputed whether predator inspection is a PD.
claims.source_title: Lazarus & Metcalfe 1990, Anim Behav 39(5):987-988 (bibliographic record)
claims.notes: Only the bibliographic record and the reply title were confirmed. The arguments of the critique were not read. Carter 2014 cites Dugatkin 1991 'Predator inspection, tit-for-tat and shoaling: A comment on Masters & Waite'.

claims.claim: Clutton-Brock (Nature 2009 review): firm evidence of reciprocity in animal societies is rare. Many examples of cooperation between non-kin are probably intra-specific mutualism or manipulation.
claims.quote: Firm evidence of reciprocity in animal societies is rare and many examples of cooperation between non-kin probably represent cases of intra-specific mutualism or manipulation.
claims.source_title: Clutton-Brock, Cooperation between non-kin in animal societies, Nature 462:51-57
claims.notes: Published November 2009. Nature's editorial summary adds: 'there is little evidence that, under natural conditions, animals other than man commonly exchange either resources or services.' That line is the editor's summary, not the author's abstract.

claims.claim: Hammerstein (2003, Dahlem volume chapter) argues that after three decades of research, only a modest number of animal examples of reciprocity exist, and evidence is scarce even in primates. Simple repeated-game models do not reflect natural conditions: most repeated animal interactions are not even repeated games, and partner switching and mobility undermine the stability of reciprocity.
claims.quote: Most repeated animal interactions do not even correspond to repeated games.
claims.source_title: Hammerstein, Why Is Reciprocity So Rare in Social Animals? A Protestant Appeal, in Genetic and Cultural Evolution of Cooperation (MIT Press), pp. 83-94
claims.notes: The PDF is a poor OCR scan. The quote was reconstructed from garbled OCR ('I.... pc.lted animal lllie raciions do not c\'en correspond 10 repealed gamt.'S'), so treat its wording as near-verbatim and check it against a clean copy. The same abstract says 'Tit-for-Tat-like behavior' has been the prime explanation 'In contrast to the shortage of support', and 'In the few known examples, quick retaliation seems to be the rule'.

claims.claim: Stevens & Hauser (TICS 2004): despite heavy theoretical interest, there is little empirical evidence for reciprocal altruism in non-human animals. They propose that cognitive constraints (temporal discounting, numerical discrimination, memory) make reciprocity hard for animals.
claims.quote: Despite immense theoretical interest, little empirical evidence substantiates the biological importance of reciprocal altruism in non-human animals.
claims.source_title: Stevens & Hauser, Why be nice? Psychological constraints on the evolution of cooperation, Trends Cogn Sci 8(2):60-65
claims.notes: Abstract via Europe PMC. The volume and pages (8(2):60-65) are from memory. Hauser later had misconduct findings (2010-2012) on other papers. Not known to affect this review, but worth noting if he is named.

claims.claim: Carter (2014, 'The reciprocity controversy'): many reviews now conclude that reciprocity is rare or absent outside humans. Carter argues this is largely semantic. Definitions translated from TFT 'basically define reciprocity out of existence', while the original broad concept is well supported in fungi, plants, fish, birds, rats and primates.
claims.quote: many reviews now conclude that it is rare or absent outside of humans. Here, I show that nonhuman reciprocity seems rare mainly because its meaning has changed over time.
claims.source_title: Carter, The Reciprocity Controversy, Animal Behavior and Cognition 1(3):368-386, doi:10.12966/abc.08.11.2014
claims.notes: Key counterpoint: the 'rare' verdict depends on taking TFT as the operational definition. Lists four problematic approaches: assuming sophisticated cognition, focusing only on short-term contingency with a single partner, demanding a paradoxical temporary fitness cost, and assuming fixed responses.

claims.claim: Raihani & Bshary (J Evol Biol 2011): strategies based on precise accounting (TFT-style bookkeeping) are relatively uncommon in animals, perhaps because the full IPD assumptions are rarely met. Animals instead use diverse strategies: positive and negative reciprocity, and long-term 'friendships'.
claims.quote: Strategies based on precise accounting are relatively uncommon, perhaps because the full set of assumptions of the IPD model are rarely satisfied.
claims.source_title: Raihani & Bshary, Resolving the iterated prisoner's dilemma: theory and reality, J Evol Biol
claims.notes: Abstract via Europe PMC.

claims.claim: Schweinfurth & Call (Learning & Behavior 2019) review three textbook cases (Norway rat, common vampire bat, brown capuchin). They conclude that many species have the psychological processes for some form of reciprocity, which 'might be a widespread phenomenon' varying in strategies and mechanisms. This is the current revisionist consensus.
claims.quote: We conclude that many species possess the psychological processes to show some form of reciprocity. Hence, reciprocity might be a widespread phenomenon that varies in terms of strategies and mechanisms.
claims.source_title: Schweinfurth & Call, Reciprocity: Different behavioural strategies, cognitive mechanisms and psychological processes, Learning & Behavior
claims.notes: The abstract also frames the split: 'some scientists conclude that reciprocity is an almost uniquely human trait ... Others, however, conclude that reciprocity is widespread'.

claims.claim: Rat evidence: Rutte & Taborsky (PLoS Biol 2007) show 'generalized reciprocity'. Female rats pulled more for an unknown partner after having been helped, regardless of partner identity. Dolivo & Taborsky (Biol Lett 2015) report that rats use direct-reciprocity rules in an IPD variant, preferentially helping cooperators over defectors, and adjust help to the quality of help received.
claims.quote: Previous experiments have demonstrated that Norway rats, Rattus norvegicus, cooperate using direct reciprocity decision rules in a variant of the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, where they preferentially help cooperators instead of defectors.
claims.source_title: Dolivo & Taborsky, Norway rats reciprocate help according to the quality of help they received, Biol Lett; Rutte & Taborsky 2007 PLoS Biol doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.0050196
claims.notes: Both abstracts via Europe PMC. Generalized reciprocity ('help anyone if helped') is not TFT, since it carries no partner-specific memory.

claims.claim: Axelrod's Ch. 4 builds on the work of Tony Ashworth, whom he calls 'a British sociologist'. Ashworth's 1980 book drew on diaries, letters and reminiscences from virtually every one of the 57 British divisions, averaging more than 3 sources per division. Axelrod says he relies on Ashworth 'for its illustrative quotes and for its historical interpretation' and admits that 'Ashworth does not put it this way' (i.e. as an iterated PD).
claims.quote: This chapter relies upon Ashworth’s fine work for its illustrative quotes and for its historical interpretation. While Ashworth does not put it this way, the historical situation in the quiet sectors along the Western Front was an iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma.
claims.source_title: Axelrod, The Evolution of Cooperation (1984), Ch. 4 'The Live-and-Let-Live System in Trench Warfare in World War I' (excerpt mirrored on gwern.net)
claims.notes: Ashworth, Trench Warfare 1914-1918: The Live and Let Live System (London: Macmillan, 1980; Pan reprint 2000). Full quote verified against the gwern excerpt (excerpt mirror, not the printed book; page numbers unverified).

claims.claim: In Ch. 4 Axelrod himself notes three departures from pure TFT. (1) Retaliation was often 'two-for-one or three-for-one'. (2) Ethics and ritual emerged, so preferences changed: 'behavior and outcomes also affected preferences'. (3) The system was ended by high-command raids, not by internal collapse.
claims.quote: When a defection actually occurred, the retaliation was often more than would be called for by TIT FOR TAT. Two-for-one or three-for-one was a common response to an act that went beyond what was considered acceptable.
claims.source_title: Axelrod 1984, Ch. 4 (excerpt)
claims.notes: Same chapter on raids: 'the high command effectively ended the live-and-let-live system by preventing their battalions from exercising their own strategies of cooperation based on reciprocity.'

claims.claim: Gelman (2008) argues that Axelrod's trench-warfare analysis 'is in error'. Western Front soldiers were not generally in a PD (iterated or otherwise), and their restraint is explained more parsimoniously as immediately reducing their own risks. Gelman is a statistician and political scientist, not a WWI historian.
claims.quote: Contrary to Axelrod’s claims, there soldiers in the Western Front were not generally in a prisoner’s dilemma (iterated or otherwise), and their cooperative behavior can be explained much more parsimoniously as immediately reducing their risks.
claims.source_title: Gelman, Methodology as ideology: mathematical modeling of trench warfare (a.k.a. 'some comments on Robert Axelrod's The Evolution of Cooperation'), QA - Rivista dell'Associazione Rossi-Doria
claims.notes: Abstract via RePEc. The 'there' typo is in the original. The full text is paywalled at FrancoAngeli. Joanne Gowa's 1986 International Organization review of Axelrod (IO 40(1):167-186) is also cited as a critique, but its text was not read.

claims.claim: Akata et al.: different LLMs (GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and others) played FINITELY repeated 2x2 games (10 rounds, horizon known) with each other, with simple strategies and with humans. LLMs do well in self-interested games such as the PD family but poorly in coordination games such as Battle of the Sexes. Preprint arXiv 2305.16867 (v1 26 May 2023, v2 7 May 2025). Published in Nature Human Behaviour 9(7):1380-1390, online 8 May 2025.
claims.quote: Here we let different LLMs play finitely repeated 2 × 2 games with each other, with human-like strategies, and actual human players. Our results show that LLMs perform particularly well at self-interested games such as the iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma family. However, they behave suboptimally in games that require coordination, such as the Battle of the Sexes.
claims.source_title: Akata, Schulz, Coda-Forno, Oh, Bethge & Schulz, Playing repeated games with large language models, Nature Human Behaviour
claims.notes: NHB metadata (vol 9, issue 7, pp. 1380-1390, online 2025-05-08) checked from the nature.com meta tags. Key caveat: with a known 10-round horizon, backward induction makes defection an equilibrium, which the authors acknowledge.

claims.claim: Akata et al.: GPT-4 'never cooperates again' against an agent that defects once and then cooperates every round after (Grim-like, unforgiving). This held across robustness checks. Told explicitly that the opponent would defect once and otherwise cooperate, GPT-4 defected in all rounds. Telling it that the other player can make mistakes (after Fudenberg et al. 2012) made it start cooperating again.
claims.quote: Crucially, GPT-4 never cooperates again when playing with an agent that defects once but then cooperates on every round thereafter. Thus, GPT-4 seems to be rather unforgiving in this setup.
claims.source_title: Akata et al., arXiv 2305.16867v2
claims.notes: From the v2 PDF text. The intro also says: 'GPT-4 retaliates repeatedly, even after only having experienced one defection ... it is particularly unforgiving and selfish.' The authors stress that defection can be the equilibrium in a known finite horizon, so 'unforgiving' is not necessarily irrational.

claims.claim: Fontana, Pierri & Aiello ('Nicer Than Humans', arXiv 2406.13605): Llama2, Llama3 and GPT-3.5 played 100-round IPDs against random opponents with varied defection rates. No model initiates defection. LLMs are at least as cooperative as typical humans. Llama2 and GPT-3.5 are more cooperative than humans and especially forgiving when opponent defection is below 30%. Llama3 is more human-like: uncooperative and exploitative unless the opponent always cooperates.
claims.quote: In particular, Llama2 and GPT3.5 are more cooperative than humans, and especially forgiving and non-retaliatory for opponent defection rates below 30%. More similar to humans, Llama3 exhibits consistently uncooperative and exploitative behavior unless the opponent always cooperates.
claims.source_title: Fontana, Pierri & Aiello, Nicer Than Humans: How do Large Language Models Behave in the Prisoner's Dilemma?
claims.notes: v1 19 Jun 2024, v2 19 Sep 2024. Journal or conference venue not verified (possibly ICWSM 2025). The opponents are random (memoryless), not reciprocal strategies.

claims.claim: Payne & Alloui-Cros (arXiv 2507.02618, v1 3 Jul 2025) ran 7 evolutionary IPD tournaments. The core is a 2x2 design: model capability (basic gpt-3.5-turbo / gemini-1.5-flash vs advanced gpt-4o-mini / gemini-2.5-flash) × per-round termination probability (10% vs 25%). Plus a 75% stress test, a 10% run with Random mutation, and a 10% 'LLM Showdown' adding claude-3-haiku-20240307. Each tournament has 24 agents, 276 round-robin matches per phase and 5 phases, with matches capped at 30 rounds. The runs produced 'almost 32,000 individual decisions and rationales'.
claims.quote: Each cell is executed once, yielding 276 round-robin matches per phase (with a fixed population of 24 agents) and a total of five phases per tournament.
claims.source_title: Payne & Alloui-Cros, Strategic Intelligence in Large Language Models: Evidence from evolutionary Game Theory
claims.notes: From the PDF text. Expected match lengths are 9±3, 3±1 and 1.3±0.1 rounds for p=0.10/0.25/0.75. Caveats: each condition run ONCE (no replication). The 'advanced' models are small or fast tiers. The showdown population is 20 (4 each of Anthropic/Bayesian/Gemini/OpenAI/Random). Still v1 only as of fetch, so not peer-reviewed.

claims.claim: Payne & Alloui-Cros 'strategic fingerprints': Gemini is 'strategically ruthless', OpenAI is 'highly cooperative' (catastrophic in hostile environments), and Claude is 'the most forgiving reciprocator'. Cooperation rates: in the 75% condition Gemini 2.2% vs OpenAI 95.7%. OpenAI was eliminated, and the final population was Gemini 16 + STFT 8. In the Showdown, Gemini 0.925, OpenAI 0.957, Anthropic 0.958.
claims.quote: Anthropic's Claude emerged as the most forgiving reciprocator, showing remarkable willingness to restore cooperation even after being exploited or successfully defecting.
claims.source_title: Payne & Alloui-Cros 2025, abstract + Table 13 + Table 8
claims.notes: Claude (only claude-3-haiku) appears in just ONE tournament, the Showdown. 'Most forgiving' rests on that single run. In the 75% run, average score per move was close (Gemini 2.207 vs OpenAI 2.171), yet the selection outcomes were wildly different. In the Showdown, Anthropic ended phase 5 with 5 agents and OpenAI with 3. Payne also writes that 'OpenAI has a higher raw cooperation rate than Gemini' in every experiment.

claims.claim: 2025 follow-ups. Willis, Du, Leibo & Luck (arXiv 2501.16173) prompted LLMs to write complete IPD strategies with aggressive, cooperative or neutral dispositions and ran evolutionary dynamics. Different LLMs show distinct biases in how well aggressive vs cooperative strategies do. Singh, Radhakrishna & Gulwani (arXiv 2509.04847) put LLM agents against 240 classical strategies in an Axelrod-style tournament. They report performance on par with, sometimes exceeding, the best classical strategies, plus the traits niceness, provocability and generosity, and detection of mid-game strategy switches within a few rounds.
claims.quote: We pit model-based agents against a suite of 240 well-established classical strategies in an Axelrod-style tournament and find that language models achieve performance on par with, and in some cases exceeding, the best-known classical strategies.
claims.source_title: Singh, Radhakrishna & Gulwani, Collaboration and Conflict between Humans and Language Models through the Lens of Game Theory (5 Sep 2025); Willis et al., Will Systems of LLM Agents Cooperate (27 Jan 2025)
claims.notes: Only the abstracts were read. Singh et al. are at Microsoft. The '240 strategies' likely means the Axelrod Python library. Which LLMs were used and the exact rankings were not checked.

claims.claim: FAIRGAME (Buscemi, Proverbio, Di Stefano, Han, Castignani & Liò; arXiv 2504.14325, v1 19 Apr 2025, v5 16 Mar 2026) is a framework for running game-theoretic games among LLM agents. It reports biased outcomes depending on the LLM, the prompt language, and the agents' personality or strategic knowledge.
claims.quote: we employ it to uncover biased outcomes in popular games among AI agents, depending on the employed Large Language Model (LLM) and used language, as well as on the personality trait or strategic knowledge of the agents.
claims.source_title: FAIRGAME: a Framework for AI Agents Bias Recognition using Game Theory
claims.notes: Abstract only. It is a tooling paper, and no specific IPD numbers were captured.

open_questions: FRD 2012 exact parameters (noise 1/8? b/c values 1.5/2/2.5/4?) and per-treatment cooperation rates: the full text was unreachable (Harvard DASH 429). Check via the AER PDF or the openICPSR replication data (project 112512).

Dal Bó & Fréchette JEL 2018 final text: all survey numbers come from the March 2016 draft (Wayback). Confirm the 15 papers / 32 treatments / 2,415 subjects and the '15 of 17 treatments' strategy figure in the published version.
Whether any professional WWI historian (as opposed to Gelman, a statistician, or Gowa, a political scientist) has critiqued Axelrod's use of Ashworth. Not found. Ashworth himself was a sociologist.
Gowa 1986 IO review: what it actually says about the trench case. Not read.

Lazarus & Metcalfe 1990 and Masters & Waite 1990: the substance of the stickleback critiques was not read. Also later Milinski/Dugatkin follow-ups (guppies, 'Tit for Tat: sticklebacks trusting a cooperating partner').
Payne & Alloui-Cros: has a peer-reviewed version appeared? arXiv still showed v1 only at fetch time. The 'Claude most forgiving' claim rests on one run with claude-3-haiku.
Akata et al.: the exact model list in the final NHB version (the abstract says 'different LLMs'; the preprint used GPT-3/3.5/4 and others) and the human-participant N for the SCoT experiment.
Wilkinson 1984: exact captive-experiment N and the 'index of opportunity for reciprocation' definition. Abstract only.
Breitmoser 2015 AER 'Cooperation, but no reciprocity: Individual strategies in the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma' is a direct counterclaim to the human-TFT evidence. Not fetched; worth adding.
